name: Privacy for Students With Disabilities
title: Privacy for Students With Disabilities
answer: Privacy for students with disabilities means treating disability information as some of the most sensitive data a school holds, so that every AI tool touching special education data is covered by a signed data privacy agreement and identifying details are removed before any tool sees them. It matters because evaluation results, diagnoses, and behavior records can follow a student for years if shared carelessly, and because trust between families and schools is hard to build and easy to lose.

sections.body: Disability information is among the most sensitive data a school holds, and it includes evaluation results, diagnoses, and behavior records that can follow a student for years when shared carelessly. The idea sets a simple rule: any AI tool that touches special education data must be covered by a signed data privacy agreement, and tools without that coverage should never see identifying information about a student with a disability. It also asks teachers to build a name removal habit, describing needs in general terms rather than naming students or giving birth dates, school names, or rare details. The problem it solves is the quiet spread of sensitive records through tools that were never approved to hold them, especially in small schools where even a grade and a disability together can point to one child. The guiding rule is that when in doubt, leave it out.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day work, a teacher who wants help with a goal or a behavior plan describes the need in general terms, leaving out names, birth dates, school names, and rare details that could identify the student. Before any AI tool is used with special education information, staff check that a signed data privacy agreement covers it, and tools without that coverage are kept away from identifying information. The text does not give separate steps by grade band, so the same habit applies wherever a student has an IEP or a behavior plan. Families are also brought in: a short list shared at the annual IEP meeting explains which tools handle their child's special education information, what each tool does, and how the district protects the data. Families who ask questions deserve clear answers.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It rests on practice and on the judgment that disability information is highly sensitive and that careless sharing can follow a student for years. The chapter points back to the data privacy agreement described in Chapter 3 as the required coverage for any tool touching special education data. It also states plainly that trust between families and schools is hard to build and easy to lose, which is offered as the reason for the practice rather than as a research finding.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set by the sensitivity of the data and by the coverage rule: tools not covered by a signed data privacy agreement should never see identifying information about a student with a disability. The name removal habit is the main safeguard, and it means leaving out names, birth dates, school names, and rare details, because in a small school even a combination of grade and disability can point to one child. When in doubt, the decision stays with the person to leave the detail out rather than include it. Families should know which tools handle their child's special education information, and the decision to share that short list at the annual IEP meeting stays with the school. Clear answers to family questions remain a human responsibility, not something delegated to a tool.
